newsitem.title: USA: Swiss defend their record on Nazi gold scandal.
newsitem.headline: Swiss defend their record on Nazi gold scandal.

text.p: A Swiss official on Thursday vigorously defended his country's response to the dispute over the Swiss purchase of Nazi gold and told the U.S. Senate his country should not be treated as "an international outcast."

Ambassador Thomas Borer, head of a Swiss Foreign Ministry task force untangling Swiss business dealings with the Nazis during the Second World War and what it did with Nazi gold after the war, made his case in testimony prepared for a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee.

Listing the attempts under way to clear up the record and begin some restitution, Borer said, "The Swiss, old and young alike ... are perplexed and wonder why, in spite of these efforts, they continue to be treated as an international outcast."

"It would indeed be tragic for all concerned if the numerous individual and collective initiatives taken nationwide in my country should be discouraged and dampened by this harsh and negative campaign."
Committee members acknowledged the steps Switzerland had taken so far but demanded more accountability.

"History is offering you at this moment what it offers very few nations throughout history -- a chance to make amends for past wrongs," said Sen. Chris Dodd, a Connecticut Democrat whose father prosecuted Nazi war criminals at Nuremberg.

Banking committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican, noted that some critics of Switzerland have floated the idea of freezing a portion of the $86 billion in Swiss assets in the United States. D'Amato said that would be "premature" and he would not support it "at this time."

D'Amato and other panel members, as well as the senior U.S. Commerce official who last week issued a report on Nazi assets, noted that several other countries who were neutral during the Second World War needed to provide an accounting.

Those nations include Sweden, Spain, Portugal, Turkey and Argentina. U.S. Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat said his report showed that their financial involvement with the Nazi war machine was neither as vast nor as pivotal as that of the Swiss.

Eizenstat's report said Switzerland handed over to the Allies just $58 million worth of Nazi gold after the war, although there may have been more than $400 million -- $4 billion in today's dollars -- in German-looted gold in Switzerland at the time.
It said some gold the Nazis sold to the Swiss was taken from Holocaust victims, even from their teeth.

Eizenstat, in his testimony on Thursday, repeated his call for all nations -- including the Allies who conquered Hitler -- to open their archives and establish not only the wartime transactions but what happened in the post-war period.
The hearing was packed with ageing orthodox Jews in their distinctive black garb and representatives of many international Jewish organisations.

Borer said Swiss authorities were still reviewing Eizenstat's report, but said it appeared Switzerland's "extremely difficult situation" militarily and economically during the war had not been adequately addressed.

Switzerland's policy at that time "constituted a tightrope walk to spare the country and its people, including the many thousands of refugees on its soil, from the war, and to preserve freedom and democracy."
Responding to an international furore over the issue, the Swiss government set up a Holocaust memorial fund with $182 million in donations from banks and businesses.

The Swiss president also proposed a $4.7 billion "Solidarity Foundation" that would finance aid to victims of disasters and human rights outrages, including the Holocaust, but made it subject to voter approval in a referendum.

Switzerland has a historical commission investigating the Swiss role as a financial centre during the war, and a banking commission with the mandate to search for unclaimed accounts of Holocaust survivors.
